Christopher Froschauer
kris'tō-fer frosh'ou-er
n. (Christopher Froschauer, c. 1490–1564, printer of Zurich)
Greek Christophoros, Christ-bearer; German Froschauer, from a Bavarian place-name, frog meadow.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Christopher Froschauer was Zwingli's printer and the press of the Zurich Reformation. In March 1522 he served sausages to a company that included Zwingli during Lent, and the ensuing uproar — the affair of the sausages — is conventionally where the Swiss Reformation begins; Froschauer's defence was that his workmen were exhausted from printing the epistles of Paul and needed feeding. He printed Zwingli's works, Bullinger's, the first Zurich Bible of 1531 — a complete German Bible five years ahead of Luther's finished version, translated by the Zurich ministers — and some nine hundred titles in all. The Froschauer Bibles were well made and cheap enough to sell, and they went into Anabaptist as well as Reformed households; the Swiss Brethren carried them to America. A press is a pulpit with a longer reach and no congregation of its own. “And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans” (Col 4:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Lent as the quadragesimal fast, and abstinence as the refraining from an indulgence of appetite.

expand to see more

LENT, n. The quadragesimal fast, or a fast of forty days, observed by the christian church before Easter.

AB'STINENCE, n. The act or practice of voluntarily refraining from any action; particularly, the refraining from an indulgence of appetite.

IM'PRINT, n. The name of the printer and the place and date of publication, printed in a book.

QUAR'TO, n. A book of the size of the fourth of a sheet; a size made by twice folding a sheet.

Modern Corruption

Zwingli's printer, the affair of the sausages, and the Zurich Bible of 1531.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the retelling of the Lenten sausages as a piece of coarse provocation, a stunt that happened to start a reformation. The point at issue was precise and the participants knew it: whether the church may bind the conscience with a rule about food that Scripture does not impose. Froschauer's men had been working long hours on the epistles of Paul, which is where the answer is.

The principle to recover is that the apostle forbids exactly this kind of binding, by name and by category. “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days” (Col 2:16). The reason is that the kingdom does not consist in such things: “For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost” (Rom 14:17). And the creature is cleared with one condition attached: “if it be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:4).

Usage

"“Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink” (Col 2:16) — Zurich, Lent 1522."

"“the kingdom of God is not meat and drink” (Rom 14:17) — the affair of the sausages."

"“cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans” (Col 4:16) — the Zurich Bible of 1531."
